summary: This unit teaches you to look after wigs and hair pieces for clients: know the types and the difference between human hair and synthetic fibre, take head measurements and fit a wig comfortably over braided natural hair, receive, clean, condition, dry, style and repair wigs, work safely with adhesives and heat, and advise clients on wearing, storing and caring for a wig without harming their own hair and scalp.

blocks.p: Wigs and hair pieces are part of everyday life in Jamaican salons. Clients wear them for fashion, for convenience in the heat, to protect their own hair, for work, for a wedding, or because of hair loss from illness or treatment. A wig is an expensive item and it sits against the client's scalp, so the way you receive, clean, style and fit it matters for her money, her appearance and the health of her own hair. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees.

You will work on wigs on blocks and on clients' heads. The two big ideas are: **know what the wig is made of** (human hair or synthetic fibre), because that decides how you wash, dry and style it; and **protect the client's own hair and scalp**, because tight braids, glue and caps can cause lasting damage.

sections.title: Types of wigs and hair pieces

head: Item
What it is
Typical use
rows: Full wig
Covers the whole head.
Complete change of look, hair loss, protective style.
Half wig (demi-wig)
Covers the back and crown, leaving the front hair out to blend in.
Adds length and volume; the client's own front hair shows.
Fall
A long hair piece attached at the crown to add length at the back.
Length for a style without a full wig.
Wiglet
A small piece used to add height or volume at the crown or elsewhere.
Volume for up-dos.
Toupee
A small piece covering the top of the head, usually for a man.
Covering a thinning crown.
Extensions and wefts
A weft is a strip of hair sewn together along the top; it is sewn, glued or clipped in.
Length and volume; wefts are also used to make wigs and sew-ins.
Closure
A small lace or silk piece that covers the parting area and finishes a wig or sew-in.
Finishing the top of a style.
Frontal
A lace piece that runs from ear to ear along the front hairline.
A natural hairline with parting options.

head: Cap
How it is made
In Jamaica's heat
rows: Capless (open-wefted)
Rows of wefts sewn on elastic bands, with gaps in between.
Usually the coolest and lightest; air circulates.
Lace-front
A fine lace panel at the front hairline, the rest a standard cap.
Natural-looking hairline; warmer than capless.
Full lace
A lace cap with hair knotted by hand.
Most natural and the most delicate; expensive; can be parted anywhere.
Monofilament (mono) top
A fine mesh at the top of the cap with hairs hand-tied, looks like a scalp.
Natural parting; costs more.
Traditional (wefted) cap
Wefts sewn to the cap, usually with a closed cap.
Durable and cheap; warmest.

ul: **Adjustable straps** at the nape and **combs or clips** inside the cap help the wig stay on.
A **custom** wig is made to the client's own head measurements. A **stock** wig comes in standard sizes (small, medium, large) and can often be adjusted with the straps.
Lace is delicate. The knots that hold the hair to the lace can pull out, and the lace tears easily.

head: Feature
Human hair
Synthetic (standard)
rows: Look and feel
Natural movement and shine; varies a little from strand to strand.
Often very shiny and smooth, the same from root to end.
Price
Costs more.
Costs less.
Life
Lasts longer with good care.
Shorter life; frizzes and thins with wear.
Styling
Can be set, blow-dried and curled with heat (use a heat protectant), and coloured with care.
Keeps its factory style after washing. Cannot be coloured with ordinary hair colour. Heat frizzes or melts it unless the maker says it is heat-resistant.
Washing
Like natural hair, with care; must be restyled after washing.
Cool water and a shampoo made for synthetic fibre; the style stays.
Drying
Blot; air dry on a stand or dry on low heat.
Blot and air dry on a stand, away from heat and sun.

ul: **Heat-resistant synthetic** fibre can take low heat, but only to the temperature the maker gives. If you do not know, treat it as ordinary synthetic.
**Remy hair** is human hair whose cuticles all lie in the same direction, root to tip, so it tangles less and shines more. Non-remy hair has mixed directions, tangles and mats.
Human hair wigs are often made from hair that has already been processed or coloured, so results vary when you colour or style them.

flow: Read the label and the maker's information; ask the client what she was told
Look and feel: shine, smoothness, texture
If still unsure, do a burn test on a few loose strands, with the instructor present

head: Test
Human hair
Synthetic fibre
rows: Burn test
Burns slowly; smells like burnt feathers; leaves a soft ash that crumbles.
Melts and shrinks away quickly, forming a hard bead; smells like plastic.
Heat
Takes heat styling with protectant.
Frizzes or melts.
Wet
Behaves like natural hair; stretches, then springs back.
Wet fibre stretches and frizzes if brushed hard.

blocks.note: Do the burn test only with the instructor present. Take a few loose strands from a hidden place such as inside a weft, hold them with tweezers over a metal dish, away from anything that can burn, in a ventilated area with your hair tied back. Never burn a piece of the visible wig.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Why does this matter? Because the wrong method ruins the wig. Hot water, hot tools or ordinary colour on a synthetic wig will frizz, melt or fail to work, and the client has to pay for a new wig.

Measure before you order, choose or adjust a wig, so that it fits without slipping or squeezing. Sit the client upright. Comb her hair flat, or braid it down if she will wear the wig over braids, so that the measurements match how the wig will sit. Use a **soft tape measure**, snug but not tight, and write measurements in **centimetres**.

head: Measurement
Where it is taken
rows: Circumference
All the way round the head: along the front hairline, behind the ears and across the nape.
Front to nape
From the front hairline, over the top of the head, to the nape.
Ear to ear over the top
From one ear, over the crown, to the other ear.
Ear to ear across the forehead
Across the forehead along the hairline, from ear to ear.
Temple to temple round the back
From one temple round the back of the head to the other.
Nape width
Across the nape from one side to the other.

ul: Write each measurement on the record card at once, with the date and the client's name.
Re-measure anything that looks unusual.
Use the measurements to choose or order the right cap size.
Check the **scalp and edges first**. Do not fit a wig over a rash, sores, signs of infection or active hair loss: refer her to a doctor.
Make sure her hair is clean, moisturised and gently detangled.
Cornrow or braid the hair **flat, going back**, in neat rows with **low tension**, especially at the edges. Tight braids cause traction alopecia.
Flatten and tuck the ends. Keep the base thin and even so that the wig lies smoothly.
Put on a **clean wig cap** or liner over the braids. Use a clean cap for every client who tries on wigs; it stops germs and sweat passing between clients.

flow: Check the scalp; put on the wig cap
Place the wig at the front hairline, then pull it back over the head and down to the nape
Check it sits evenly, with the hairline and ears matched on both sides
Adjust the straps at the nape so it is snug but not tight
Fix the combs or clips into the braids, not into the edges
Trim the lace or style the hairline as needed
Check the client is comfortable; show her the back and sides in a mirror

head: Fitting problem
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Wig slips back
Cap too big; straps loose; slippery cap
Tighten the adjustable straps; secure the combs or clips; a grip band if the Centre allows
Wig squeezes or gives a headache
Cap too small; straps too tight; tight braids
Loosen the straps; re-measure; check the braid tension; choose a larger cap
Lace shows or lifts at the front
Wrong cap or poor placement
Re-place from the front hairline; trim and blend the lace; do not glue without a patch test
Wig looks bulky on top
Braids too thick or not flat
Re-do the braids flatter and thinner

ul: Do a **patch test** before using an adhesive on a client for the first time, as the maker says. Any reaction means no adhesive.
Check that the skin along the hairline has no cuts, spots or rashes. Clean the skin so the adhesive holds.
Apply a **thin layer**, keep it off the client's own hair and eyes, and let it set as the maker says.
Work in a **well-ventilated** area: fumes irritate the eyes and lungs. Many adhesives and removers are flammable: keep them away from flames and hot tools.
To remove a wig, **soften** the adhesive with the maker's remover and lift the lace gently. Never pull it off.
Close containers tightly and store them in a cool place. Wear gloves.

blocks.note: A glued wig worn for weeks, with tight braids and a daily hot head, is a common cause of thinning at the front hairline. Advise rest for the edges, no glue on thin areas, and a wig that can be removed at night.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Receiving, cleaning and conditioning a wig

ul: **Label** the wig with the client's name and the date, with a tag or a note, so that it cannot be mixed up with another.
**Note its condition** on a condition sheet: loose wefts, tears in the lace, matting, glue on the lace, shedding, missing combs, colour fade.
Ask what she wants done and what products she uses on it. Agree the work and the price.

blocks.p: A wig needs washing **after a number of wears**, sooner in hot weather, if she sweats a lot, or if she uses a lot of product. Sweat, oil, dust and products build up inside the cap and on the hair. A dirty wig smells, tangles and wears out.

flow: Remove adhesive from the lace with the maker's remover; wear gloves
Detangle gently with a wide-tooth comb, from the ends up, holding the hair near the cap
Fill a basin with lukewarm water and a mild shampoo
Swish the wig gently; run shampoo down the hair with your fingers; do not rub, twist or scrub the lace
Rinse in clean, cool water until clear
Apply conditioner from the mid-lengths to the ends, keeping it off the knots in the lace; leave it as the maker says; rinse
Blot in a towel, never wring
Put it on a wig stand or block to air dry, or dry on low heat; then style
Detangle gently, from the ends up, with a wide-tooth comb or wig brush
Use cool water (not warm or hot) and a shampoo made for synthetic wigs
Soak briefly and swish gently; do not rub
Rinse in cool water
Use a conditioner or spray made for synthetic fibre
Blot with a towel; air dry on a stand, away from sun and heat
Once dry, shake out and comb gently into style

head: Rule
Reason
rows: Detangle from the ends up
Combing from the roots pushes knots down into a bigger tangle and tears the wefts or the lace knots.
Cool to lukewarm water
Heat frizzes synthetic fibre and can dry human hair and loosen the glue or knots.
Swish, do not rub
Rubbing tangles and matts the hair and tears the lace.
Do not brush hard when wet
Wet synthetic fibre stretches and frizzes; wet human hair stretches and breaks.
A shampoo made for the fibre
Strong shampoos and dish soap dry and dull the fibre.
Blot, do not wring; dry on a stand
Wringing twists the hair and the cap; a stand keeps the shape.
Keep conditioner off the lace
It makes the knots slip and loosens the hair.

ul: Handle the lace at the front **gently**. The lace and the knots tear easily.
A light **leave-in conditioner** helps keep a human hair wig soft between washes.
If you tear the lace by accident, **tell the instructor and the client honestly**. A hidden tear gets worse, and trust is lost.

blocks.p: A **block** (canvas head form) holds the wig in shape while you work on it. Choose a block that matches the wig's cap size. Fix it to a table or trolley with a **clamp**. Put the wig on, line up the front hairline, and hold it firmly with **T-pins** (blocking pins) at the front, the sides and the nape. Cover the block with plastic wrap or a clean cap if it is shared.

blocks.note: T-pins and needles: count them before and after, keep them in a box, never hold them in your mouth, and never leave one in a wig. Broken needles and blades go in a sharps box.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Method
Human hair wig
Synthetic wig
rows: Heat tools
Yes, with a heat protectant. Test the iron on a tissue or towel first; use small sections and a heat to suit the hair.
No, unless the maker says the fibre is heat-resistant, and then only to the temperature given.
Roller set
Wet set, dry on low heat or air dry.
Wet set on rollers and leave to dry fully. This is the usual way to curl a standard synthetic wig.
Blow-dry
Yes, on a medium heat with protectant.
Cool air only, or none.
Colour
Possible, with a strand test, because the hair is often already treated.
Hair colour does not work on synthetic fibre; do not try.
Cutting
Cut it on the client's head, or on a block of the same size, so that the length and shape suit how it sits.
Same.

ul: Detangle before you style. Style only when the wig is clean and dry or damp for a set.
For a curling iron on a human hair wig: protectant, a heat that suits the hair, small sections, and test the iron on a tissue first.
When cutting, cut a little at a time. A wig cannot be regrown.
Do a **strand test** first. The hair is often already coloured or processed, so results vary.
Use only colour made for the hair, as the maker says; keep colour off the lace and cap.
Remember that wig hair has no scalp heat and no natural pigment to lighten; follow the maker's advice on time and lift.
Condition afterwards.

head: Fault
Repair
rows: A weft has come loose inside the cap
Sew it back in place with a strong needle and thread, in matching colour.
A comb or clip has come off
Sew in a replacement.
Elastic or strap stretched
Replace the strap or elastic.
Small hole or tear in lace
Mend carefully or send for a specialist repair; tell the client.
Matting at the nape
Soften with conditioner and detangle slowly from the ends; cut out if impossible, and tell the client.

blocks.p: If a repair is beyond you, say so. It is better to tell the client than to damage the wig.

sections.title: Hygiene, safety and the client's own hair

ul: A wig sits against the scalp, where sweat, oil and germs build up, especially in heat. Hygiene matters for the client and for other clients.
Label each wig; never mix wigs or tools between clients without cleaning them.
Use a **clean wig cap or liner** for every try-on.
Check the scalp before fitting. If there is a rash, sores or signs of infection, **do not fit the wig**: explain kindly and advise her to see a doctor.
Wash your hands before and after each service.

Clean combs and brushes of hair, wash them in warm soapy water, then **disinfect** them for the time on the label. Cover blocks. Use fresh towels for each client. Wipe the work area with disinfectant.
After a client with head lice or an infection, clean and disinfect tools and wash the capes and caps.

head: Hazard
Prevention
rows: Flame in the burn test
Instructor present; metal dish; away from anything flammable; hair tied back; ventilated.
Hot tools
Check cords and plugs; test on a tissue; rest tools on a heat mat; never leave them on.
Adhesive fumes and fire
Ventilation; keep away from flames; gloves; patch test.
T-pins and needles
Count them; keep in a box; sharps box for broken ones.
Wet floor
Wipe up water at once; dry your hands before plugs.
Strained back and neck
Work at a good height; adjust the block and chair.

ul: Keep her scalp clean and her hair moisturised under a wig. Wash and condition her own hair regularly.
Braid down with **low tension**; avoid tight bands, glue at the edges and constant pulling.
Give her hair and her edges **rest**: remove the wig at night, and take breaks from wigs.
Check the hairline each visit. If thinning, broken hairs or bumps appear, advise rest and, if it does not improve, a doctor.
Do not put combs or clips into the edges.

blocks.note: Traction alopecia from tight braids and glue can become permanent. Early advice saves a client's hairline.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Store it on a **wig stand**, or in a box or a satin bag, away from heat, direct sun, dust and damp.
Never store a damp wig in a bag or box: it will smell and grow mildew.
Keep synthetic wigs away from heat from ovens, grills and hot dryers: a blast of heat can frizz or melt the fibres.
Keep wigs away from pets and children.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Detangle gently with a wide-tooth comb or wig brush, from the ends up
Prevents tearing and matting.
Take the wig off at night; do not sleep in it unless it is made for it
Friction tangles it and the scalp needs air.
Wash after a number of wears, or sooner in heat, with the right products and water
Removes sweat, oil and build-up.
Use only light products
Heavy products build up and weigh the hair down.
Keep synthetic wigs from heat sources
Fibre frizzes or melts.
Look after her own scalp and hair under the wig
Keeps the hair healthy and prevents hair loss.
Come back if she sees damage, hair loss or soreness
Early help prevents bigger problems.

ul: Write the wig's details: type, fibre, cap, colour, condition.
Record head measurements in centimetres, with the date.
Record the care given and the products used.
Note any damage found, any advice given and the client's agreement.
Keep records confidential and store them safely.

blocks.p: Records mean the next stylist uses the right care. They also show what condition the wig was in when it came, which settles disagreements.

ul: I can name full wigs, half wigs, falls, wiglets, toupees, wefts, closures and frontals, and say what each is for.
I can describe capless, lace-front, full lace, monofilament and traditional caps.
I can compare human hair and synthetic wigs for look, price, life, styling and care.
I can identify the fibre by label, look and feel, and a safe supervised burn test.
I can take head measurements in centimetres with a soft tape and record them.
I can check the scalp, braid the natural hair flat with low tension, and fit and secure a wig with a clean cap.
I can solve slipping and squeezing problems.
I can use lace adhesives and removers safely, including the patch test.
I can receive, label and record the condition of a wig.
I can clean and condition a human hair wig and a synthetic wig correctly.
I can block a wig and pin it, and count the T-pins afterwards.
I can style a human hair wig with heat and a synthetic wig with a wet set.
I can do simple repairs and tell the client honestly when I cannot.
I can keep tools, blocks and caps hygienic.
I can advise clients on wearing, storing and caring for a wig and her own hair, and fill in the record.

blocks.note: In essay answers, name the fibre and the method together: 'a synthetic wig is washed in cool water because heat frizzes the fibre.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Full wig
A wig covering the whole head.
Hair piece
A piece that covers only part of the head, such as a fall, wiglet or toupee.
Weft
A strip of hair sewn together along the top.
Closure
A small lace or silk piece covering the parting area.
Frontal
A lace piece running ear to ear along the front hairline.
Capless
A cap of wefts on elastic with open gaps; usually the coolest.
Lace front
A wig with a fine lace panel at the front hairline.
Remy hair
Human hair with all the cuticles lying in one direction.
Synthetic fibre
Man-made hair that keeps its style after washing and is damaged by heat unless heat-resistant.
Burn test
A supervised test on a few loose strands to tell human hair from synthetic.
Circumference
The measurement all the way round the head along the hairline.
Block
A canvas head form that holds a wig for styling.
T-pins
Pins that hold a wig firmly on a block.
Patch test
A small test of an adhesive on the skin before first use.
Traction alopecia
Hair loss from constant pulling on the hair.
Sharps box
A container for broken needles and used blades.

c1.title: A birthday wig in Spanish Town
c1.text: Marcia Bailey, 38, brings a long, shiny wig to a salon in Spanish Town the day before her birthday party. She cannot remember whether it is human hair or synthetic. The label is missing. She wants it washed and given big curls with a hot curling iron. Trainee Rohan notices that the wig is very smooth and shiny and feels the same from root to end. The wig has glue on the lace front, from her last party.

c2.title: A loose wig in Montego Bay
c2.text: Trainee Chanelle is fitting a lace-front wig on Patrice Francis, 45, who has thinned at the temples from wearing tight wigs with glue for years. Patrice's natural hair is in tight cornrows done by someone else. The wig slips back and Patrice says her head is sore. She suggests glue 'at the front to hold it', and she says she has never used adhesive before.

c3.title: A synthetic wig and a kitchen in Mandeville
c3.text: Lorna Brown, 52, works in a cook shop in Mandeville and wears a synthetic wig every day. She comes in with the wig frizzy at the front and ends, and a musty smell. She says she washes it in hot water with dish soap, brushes it hard when it is wet, and leaves it on the kitchen counter beside the oven.

c4.title: Measuring for a custom wig in Kingston
c4.text: Trainee Andre is measuring Nadine Reid, 29, for a custom wig. She will wear it over cornrows. He has her sit up and combs her loose hair flat, then he measures round her head with a metal ruler and writes the numbers in inches on a scrap of paper. Nadine has a sore, red patch with weeping spots at the nape.

c5.title: Styling and storage in Ocho Rios
c5.text: In the training salon in Ocho Rios, trainee Kayla is styling a human hair wig on a block. She pins it with T-pins from her mouth, uses a hot flat iron without protectant, and does not count the pins afterwards. At the end of the day she puts the damp wig into a closed plastic bag and leaves the block on a trolley in the sun.

questions.q: Marcia cannot say what her wig is made of. Which clue in the case points most to synthetic fibre?
o: There is old glue left along the lace at the front of the wig
The wig is long, and it has big loose waves all the way through
The fibre is very glossy and feels the same from root to end
She wears it only for parties and other special days
questions.why: Very glossy fibre that feels the same from root to end is typical of synthetic hair; human hair varies a little. Glue, length and how often it is worn say nothing about the fibre. If still unsure, a burn test is done with the instructor present.

questions.q: How should the burn test be done, if the instructor agrees?
o: Over a metal dish, with a few hidden strands, away from flammables
On a visible part of the front, so that the client can see the result
Over the sink, using the whole fringe, to be sure of the result
On the block with the wig pinned down, with a lighter held close
questions.why: Only a few hidden strands are used, held with tweezers over a metal dish, away from anything flammable, in a ventilated place. Burning visible hair or the lace damages the wig.

questions.q: The strands melt into a hard bead and smell like plastic. What does this tell Rohan?
o: The wig is human hair that has been treated
The wig is remy hair with the cuticles reversed
The wig is human hair, but dirty
The wig is synthetic, so no hot irons
questions.why: Synthetic fibre melts into a hard bead and smells like plastic. Human hair burns slowly with a burnt-feather smell and leaves ash. A hot iron on synthetic fibre will frizz or melt it.

questions.q: How should Rohan remove the old glue from the lace front?
o: Peel it off slowly while the lace is dry and the glue is hard
Soften it with the maker's remover and lift it gently
Soak the lace in very hot water and scrape it with a comb
Cut the lace away neatly along the edge of the glue line
questions.why: Adhesive is softened with the maker's remover and lifted gently; pulling or scraping tears the lace and knots. Gloves protect the skin and the area must be ventilated.

questions.q: What is the best first step for the wig slipping back?
o: Glue the front down firmly all along the front hairline
Tighten the straps and fix the combs into the braids
Put a second wig cap on top to make it grip better
Pull the wig forward and pin it into the temples to hold it
questions.why: Straps and combs are made to hold a wig. Glue should not be the first answer, especially with thin temples, and pins in the edges damage the hair.

questions.q: Why is Patrice's sore head probably linked to her braids?
o: The braids are too loose and rub against the cap
Cornrows always hurt when they are worn under a wig
The wig cap is far too large for her head
The braids are too tight and pull on the scalp
questions.why: Tight braids pull on the follicles, causing soreness and, over time, traction hair loss, especially at the edges. Braids should be flat with low tension.

questions.q: Before using adhesive on Patrice for the first time, what must Chanelle do?
o: Do a patch test as the maker says and check the skin
Put it along the whole hairline to see how it dries
Ask Patrice whether she has ever reacted to a food
Mix it with a little oil so that it is gentler on skin
questions.why: A patch test checks for allergy before the adhesive goes near the hairline. The skin must also be free of cuts, spots and rashes.

questions.q: Given Patrice's thinning temples, what is the best advice?
o: Glue the wig firmly at the temples so that it cannot slide
Wear tighter cornrows underneath so that it grips better
Rest the edges: no glue, looser braids, wig off at night
Stop washing her own hair, to keep the edges away from water
questions.why: Thinning at the temples is a sign of traction. Rest, low tension, no glue on thin areas and regular removal of the wig give the edges the best chance. If it does not improve she should see a doctor.

questions.q: Which care habit most likely caused Lorna's frizzy fibre?
o: Washing her own hair under the wig far more often than needed
Sleeping on a satin pillowcase with the wig tied in a scarf
Storing it on a wig stand in a cool and shaded corner
Hot water, hard brushing when wet, and heat from the oven
questions.why: Heat frizzes synthetic fibre, and wet fibre stretches and frizzes if brushed hard. A satin pillowcase and a wig stand are both good habits.

questions.q: How should the salon wash Lorna's wig?
o: In warm water with dish soap, rubbing the front well
In cool water with a synthetic shampoo, swishing gently
In hot water to remove the smell, then brushing it hard
Dry-clean it with a spray and never let it get wet
questions.why: Synthetic fibre needs cool water and a gentle shampoo made for it. Dish soap dries the fibre, and rubbing and hot water frizz it.

questions.q: Once Lorna's wig is rinsed and conditioned, what is the safe way to finish it?
o: Dry it under a hot hood dryer, turned up to its highest setting
Wring it out well, then hang it on a line in the hot sun
Blot it in a towel, then leave it on a stand out of the sun
Rub it dry with a towel and brush it out straight away
questions.why: Blot, never wring, and air dry on a stand away from heat. A hot dryer can melt synthetic fibre, and wringing or rubbing twists the hair and frizzes the fibre.

questions.q: What advice about storage and heat should the salon give Lorna?
o: Keep it away from ovens and grills, and store it on a stand
Keep it on the kitchen counter so that it is always easy to reach
It is fine to leave it near the oven as long as it is clean
Put it in a damp plastic bag overnight to keep it soft
questions.why: A blast of heat from an oven can frizz or melt synthetic fibre. Store wigs on a stand or in a box, away from heat, sun and damp.

questions.q: What should Andre have used to measure Nadine, and where should he have recorded the result?
o: A soft tape measure, with centimetres written on the record card
A metal ruler, with inches noted on a piece of scrap paper
A stiff ruler, with centimetres written on the client's receipt
A soft tape measure, with the numbers remembered until later
questions.why: Head measurements need a soft tape measure and are written in centimetres on the client's record card at once. Because Nadine will wear the wig over cornrows, her hair should also be braided down first, so that the measurements match how the wig will sit.

questions.q: What is the circumference measurement?
o: From the front hairline, over the top of the head, to the nape
From one ear to the other, across the forehead along the hairline
Right round the head, along the hairline and across the nape
Across the nape from one side to the other, below the ears
questions.why: The circumference goes right round the head along the hairline, behind the ears and across the nape. The other options are different measurements.

questions.q: What should Andre do about the sore, red patch with weeping spots at the nape?
o: Fit the wig carefully over it, using a clean wig cap
Not fit the wig; explain kindly and suggest a doctor
Cover it with a thin layer of adhesive to protect the skin
Put conditioner on the patch and carry on with the fitting
questions.why: A weeping, crusty or sore area could be an infection, and a wig or cap over it traps heat and sweat. Do not fit the wig, explain privately and suggest a doctor.

questions.q: Why are the measurements written on the record card straight away?
o: So they can be shared with other clients who ask
Because the client will then be able to change them
Because the numbers will change from week to week
So the cap size can be chosen or ordered later
questions.why: Immediate, dated records prevent errors and are used to choose or order the cap size. They also help whoever serves her next.

questions.q: What is wrong with how Kayla handled the T-pins?
o: She used T-pins to hold the wig on the block
She held pins in her mouth and never counted them
She pinned the wig at the nape as well as the sides
She pinned the wig firmly at the front hairline too
questions.why: T-pins are counted before and after, kept in a box, never held in the mouth and never left in a wig. Pinning at the front, sides and nape is correct.

questions.q: What should Kayla have done before using a flat iron on a human hair wig?
o: Put on a heat protectant and tested the iron on tissue
Set the iron to its very hottest setting so as to save time
Tested it on a hidden corner of the lace front first
Soaked the wig, then ironed the wet hair until it was dry
questions.why: Human hair can be heat-styled with a protectant and a heat to suit it. A tissue test shows if the iron is too hot. Ironing wet hair steams and damages it.

questions.q: What is the problem with the way Kayla stored the damp wig?
o: A plastic bag is ideal because it keeps the wig dry
A sunny trolley is the best place for drying a wig
A closed bag is fine for a human hair wig, though not synthetic
It can grow mildew in the closed bag; it should dry on a stand
questions.why: Damp wigs stored in a closed bag get mildew and smell. A wig should dry fully on a stand, away from direct sun and heat.

questions.q: A trainee tears the lace on a client's wig while cleaning it. What is the right thing to do?
o: Say nothing and hand it back, as the tear is only small
Cover the tear with a little adhesive and say nothing
Tell the instructor and the client, and agree a repair
Tell her the wig was old and likely to tear anyway
questions.why: Honest reporting protects the client's trust and lets a repair be planned. Hidden damage gets worse and may lead to a complaint.
